analysis.one_liner: Requires oil companies to renegotiate old royalty-free Gulf leases before winning new ones.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, has zero cosponsors, and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a 1995 law, some deepwater Gulf of Mexico oil and gas leases issued from 1996 through 2000 came with 'royalty holidays' that lacked price limits, so companies pay no royalties on a set share of production even when oil prices are high. This bill would deny those companies new Gulf leases and lease transfers until they renegotiate the old leases to pay royalties once prices pass set thresholds, and it would have the Interior Department approve amendments adding those thresholds to the old leases.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and the federal Treasury, which would collect royalties on high-priced Gulf production that currently goes to leaseholders royalty-free, along with state and conservation programs that receive federal energy royalties.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Interior Secretary from issuing any new Gulf of Mexico oil or gas lease to a company holding one of the old royalty-relief leases unless the company renegotiates it to require royalty payments when oil or gas prices reach set thresholds.

Applies the same condition to buying, selling, or otherwise transferring a covered lease or its economic benefit, including through swaps, spinoffs, or servicing agreements, closing a route around the rule.
Directs the Interior Secretary to approve any lessee's request to amend leases issued between January 1996 and November 2000 to add price thresholds, with the new terms taking effect October 1, 2026.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding the old deepwater royalty-relief leases, which would owe royalties when prices are high instead of selling that share of production free of charge.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies holding old Gulf leases

drawbacks.text: The bill retroactively rewrites the financial terms of leases companies lawfully signed under the 1995 Deep Water Royalty Relief Act, which offered royalty holidays as an incentive to take on deepwater drilling when it was expensive and unproven; companies would almost certainly challenge the forced renegotiation, and critics argue it changes the terms of past deals.

The leverage only works on companies that want a new lease or want to trade their old ones; a company content to keep producing under its existing lease without buying or selling anything faces no direct requirement to renegotiate, so the revenue recovered depends on market activity and oil prices crossing the thresholds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain is real public revenue from production that now yields nothing for taxpayers whenever prices are high, and the cost falls on a specific set of leaseholders that received an unusually favorable deal. The main risks are legal (rewriting signed contracts) and practical (the bill can only reach companies that seek new leases or transfers). On balance, the public gain likely outweighs the cost, but the design leaves obvious escape routes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee on March 11, 2025, and it has sat there since, with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill in the House on March 11, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, which has taken no further action on it.
No member of the House from either party has signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies holding the old royalty-relief leases are better off so far: with no renegotiation required, they keep selling their royalty-free share of Gulf production, and the Treasury keeps forgoing that revenue whenever prices are high.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral for offshore energy leasing legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 11, 2025 and has not scheduled it for a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes have occurred; the only recorded support is the Democratic sponsor, and no Republican and no other Democrat has cosponsored the bill.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies holding pre-2001 deepwater Gulf royalty-relief leases
industries.note: These companies currently keep the full value of a royalty-free share of their Gulf production, including when oil and gas prices spike, at a direct cost to the Treasury. The bill would make them pay royalties once prices pass thresholds and blocks new leases and lease transfers until they do.

industries.industry: Gulf of Mexico offshore oil and gas industry broadly
industries.note: Companies without one of the old covered leases face no new condition, but the industry as a whole would operate under the threat of forced renegotiation of legacy leases, which could complicate lease sales and transfers.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since referral, the bill is on track to die when this Congress ends in January 2027. Its sponsor, Rep. Grijalva, died on March 13, 2025, two days after introducing it, leaving the bill without an active champion, and stand-alone royalty overhaul bills have historically advanced only when attached to broader energy or budget legislation.
